boostHintC: Hold Boost above the brake = faster
sirkyRules2: Whoever takes the last match loses the round.
sirkyRules3: First to win 5 rounds wins the game.
okoRules1: Get closer to 21 than the banker without going over.
okoRules2: Hit takes a card, Stand ends your turn. The banker draws to 17.
okoRules3: Two cards making 21 win at once. First to 5 rounds wins.
damaRules1: Move diagonally forward; kings move any distance.
damaRules2: Capturing is compulsory and must continue while possible.
damaRules3: Win by leaving the opponent no move. After 8 minutes material decides.
desetRules1: Roll six dice and set aside scoring ones: 1 = 100, 5 = 50.
desetRules3: Bank or roll on – a roll without points loses the turn. First to 5000.
sipkyRules1: Drag to aim, release to throw. The sight sways – time it.
sipkyRules2: Count down from 301; three darts per turn. Going below zero is a bust.
sipkyRules3: Hit exactly zero before the opponent.
koulenaRules1: Flick the ball up the lane into the rings.
kulickyRules1: Flick your marble towards the hole.
kulickyRules2: A marble in the hole scores 3, otherwise the closer one scores 1.
caraRules1: Toss the coin as close to the line as you can.
caraRules2: Over the line it is burnt; right on the line scores 3.
caraRules3: Seven rounds, the closer coin takes the round.
nohejbalRules1: Swipe to send the ball into the other half.
nohejbalRules2: Out of the court is a point for your rival, out of their reach a point for you.
nohejbalRules3: First to 10 with a two-point lead.
strelniceRules1: Tap the targets as they glide by.
strelniceRules2: Small ones score most. Six shots, then a short reload.
feedHost1: I have a game for you. Coming?
feedHost2: We play for honour here. Dare you?
feedHost3: Drop by, the table is free.
feedHost4: Heard you are good. Prove it.
feedHint: Up: next · down: back · right: go · left: less · double tap: like

aboutIntro: Metropole draws real cities from open map data. Thank you to everyone who maps them.
aboutOsm: © OpenStreetMap contributors. Available under the Open Database License (ODbL 1.0).
aboutOverture: Overture Maps Foundation, overturemaps.org (release {release}). Roads, buildings, water, land use and boundaries: ODbL 1.0, they contain OpenStreetMap data.
aboutOverturePlaces: Overture places: CDLA Permissive 2.0 for most sources; Foursquare data Apache 2.0, AllThePlaces CC0 1.0. Places are used only as positions and categories, names in the game are fictional.
aboutCityData: City open data and GHSL heights are not used in this city pack yet; when a city adds them, they are listed here.
aboutShareAlike: The city packs and the pipeline that builds them are public in the source repository, so the derived map database is available under ODbL.
aboutPostcards: Postcard texts are written for the game; postcard pictures are drawn by the game, no photos are used.
lm_empire_state_text: An Art Deco giant that rose in just thirteen months and opened in 1931. Its crown is lit in different colours almost every night.
lm_chrysler_text: Stacked steel arches with triangular windows make this the shiniest crown on the skyline. For a few months in 1930 it was the tallest building in the world.
lm_grand_central_text: A great railway hall whose green ceiling is painted with the constellations. Meet under the round brass clock above the information booth.
lm_times_square_text: Screens and billboards light this crossing so brightly that night never quite falls. On New Year's Eve a glowing ball drops here at midnight.
lm_central_park_text: A park four kilometres long, shaped by hand out of swamps and rock. Lakes, meadows and stone bridges hide inside the street grid.
lm_rockefeller_text: A slender limestone tower with a lookout terrace high above Midtown. In winter the sunken plaza at its foot becomes an ice rink under a giant tree.
lm_un_hq_text: A slim slab of green glass by the East River, where the countries of the world meet. A long row of member flags lines the avenue outside.
lm_st_patricks_text: A white marble cathedral with twin Gothic spires, finished in 1878. Among the towers of Fifth Avenue it looks almost small.
lm_nypl_text: Two stone lions guard the steps of this marble library on Fifth Avenue. Its main reading room is nearly as long as a city block.
lm_carnegie_hall_text: A brick concert hall loved for its sound since 1891. Ask how to get here and a local will tell you: practise.
lm_one_wtc_text: The tallest tower in the Western Hemisphere reaches exactly 1,776 feet with its spire. The number recalls the year of American independence.
lm_wtc_memorial_text: Two square pools fill the footprints of the twin towers. Water falls without end into the voids, framed by the names of the victims.
lm_woolworth_text: A white terracotta tower nicknamed the Cathedral of Commerce, finished in 1913. Its Gothic top was once higher than any other building on Earth.
lm_city_hall_text: One of the oldest city halls in the country that still houses its government. A small park with a fountain spreads out in front of it.
lm_federal_hall_text: A temple of columns on Wall Street, where the first president took his oath. His bronze statue still watches over the steps.
lm_flatiron_text: A narrow triangle of a building where Broadway cuts across Fifth Avenue. At its sharp tip it is only about two metres wide.
lm_washington_arch_text: A marble arch at the foot of Fifth Avenue, built for the centenary of the first presidential inauguration. Street musicians play beneath it all day.
lm_high_line_text: An old freight railway lifted above the streets, now a park in the air. Wild grasses grow between the preserved rails.
lm_met_museum_text: One of the largest art museums in the world, holding five thousand years of art. Its wide steps on Fifth Avenue are a favourite meeting spot.
lm_brooklyn_bridge_text: Granite towers and a web of steel cables have carried this bridge across the East River since 1883. A wooden walkway runs above the traffic.
lm_prague_castle_text: The largest ancient castle complex in the world, with St Vitus Cathedral rising from its courtyards. Kings, emperors and presidents have ruled from here for over a thousand years.
lm_old_town_square_text: The heart of the old town since the Middle Ages, framed by pastel houses and Gothic spires. Markets, coronations and protests have all filled this square.
lm_old_town_hall_text: Its astronomical clock has told the time, the sun and the moon since 1410. Every hour a small crowd waits for the apostles to appear.
lm_tyn_church_text: Two jagged Gothic towers rise eighty metres above the square like something from a fairy tale. The church hides behind a row of houses, so you have to find its door.
lm_bridge_tower_text: This Gothic gate has guarded the end of Charles Bridge since the fourteenth century. From its gallery you see the bridge's statues lined up toward the castle.
lm_st_nicholas_text: A green dome and a bell tower crown the finest Baroque church in Malá Strana. Mozart once played its organ.
lm_wenceslas_square_text: Less a square than a broad boulevard sloping up to the National Museum. Crowds gathered here in 1918, 1968 and 1989.
lm_national_museum_text: A grand neo-Renaissance palace with a glass dome closes off the top of Wenceslas Square. Inside are fossils, minerals and a pantheon of famous Czechs.
lm_national_theatre_text: Built with money collected from ordinary people and opened in 1881, its golden roof shines over the river. When it burned down soon after, the nation paid to build it again.
lm_dancing_house_text: Two towers lean into each other on the embankment like a couple in mid-dance. It opened in 1996 and still divides opinions.
lm_powder_tower_text: This dark Gothic gate once marked the start of the royal coronation route. Its name comes from the gunpowder stored inside in the seventeenth century.
lm_municipal_house_text: An Art Nouveau jewel full of mosaics, stained glass and gilded halls. Czechoslovak independence was proclaimed here in 1918.
lm_rudolfinum_text: A neo-Renaissance concert hall on the riverbank, home of the Czech Philharmonic. Statues of composers line its roof.
lm_petrin_tower_text: A steel lattice tower on Petřín hill, inspired by the one in Paris and finished in 1891. Climb its 299 steps for a view over all the red roofs.
lm_zizkov_tower_text: A rocket-shaped tower that soars 216 metres above Žižkov. Giant sculpted babies crawl up its legs.
lm_vysehrad_text: Two slender neo-Gothic spires mark the old fortress of Vyšehrad on its rock above the Vltava. Next door, the cemetery holds many of the nation's great artists.
lm_main_station_text: Behind the modern hall hides an Art Nouveau station building with a domed café. Trains have run from here since 1871.
lm_old_new_synagogue_text: The oldest working synagogue in Europe, built in the thirteenth century. Legend says the Golem still sleeps in its attic.
lm_klementinum_text: A vast former Jesuit college with a Baroque library and an astronomical tower. Weather has been measured here every day since 1775.
lm_vitkov_text: One of the largest bronze equestrian statues in the world watches over the city from Vítkov hill. It honours the Hussite general Jan Žižka.

lm_tokyo_tower_text: A red and white lattice tower from 1958, taller than its Paris model. It still carries radio antennas and glows orange at night.
lm_skytree_text: The tallest tower in Japan at 634 metres, a number that reads like the old name of the region. Its base is a triangle that turns into a circle on the way up.
lm_kaminarimon_text: The Thunder Gate of Asakusa's oldest temple, guarded by the gods of wind and thunder. Its giant red lantern is the city's favourite photo backdrop.
lm_nakamise_text: A shopping lane that has led to Sensō-ji for about three hundred years. Stalls sell rice crackers, fans and sweet bean cakes.
lm_tokyo_station_text: A red brick station from 1914 whose domes were rebuilt after the war and restored in 2012. Behind it the bullet trains leave every few minutes.
lm_nijubashi_text: A stone bridge over the palace moat, mirrored in the water like a double bridge. Beyond it lies the residence of the emperor.
lm_kabukiza_text: The main stage of kabuki theatre, with a temple-like roof in front of a modern tower. Plays here can last most of a day.
lm_tokyo_national_museum_text: The oldest museum in Japan, in Ueno Park, full of swords, scrolls and samurai armour. The main hall wears a heavy tiled roof on a concrete body.
lm_ginza_clock_text: A curved corner building with a clock that has watched the Ginza crossing since 1932. Its chimes mark the hour above the shopping crowds.
lm_akihabara_text: Once a black market for radio parts, now a maze of electronics, games and anime shops. On Sundays the main street closes to cars.
lm_zojoji_text: A great Buddhist temple at the foot of Tokyo Tower, where six shoguns are buried. Rows of small stone statues wear knitted red caps.
lm_roppongi_hills_text: A city within the city: offices, homes, a museum on the 53rd floor and a giant spider sculpture at its feet. From the top you see Tokyo Tower up close.
lm_hamarikyu_text: A former shogun's duck-hunting garden with a seawater pond that rises and falls with the tide. Skyscrapers frame its teahouse.
lm_tokyo_dome_text: A baseball stadium under an air-supported roof that locals call the Big Egg. Concerts and fights fill it when the season ends.
lm_nihonbashi_text: The bridge from which all distances in Japan were once measured. Today it sits in the shadow of an expressway built over it in 1963.
lm_kokugikan_text: The national sumo arena, where three of the six yearly tournaments are fought. Wrestlers in light robes walk the streets around it.
lm_tsukiji_outer_text: The fish auctions moved away, but the narrow lanes of stalls stayed. Breakfast here means tamagoyaki and the freshest sushi in town.
lm_sumida_river_text: A riverside park in Asakusa with cherry trees along the Sumida. In summer the sky above it fills with fireworks.
lm_kanda_myojin_text: A shrine with more than 1,200 years of history, painted vermilion and gold. The tech crowd of nearby Akihabara comes here to bless their gadgets.
lm_budokan_text: An octagonal hall built for judo at the 1964 Olympics, its roof shaped like Mount Fuji. Later it became a legendary concert stage.
lm_akasaka_palace_text: Japan's only neo-baroque palace, built for a crown prince and now the state guest house. Kings and presidents sleep here on state visits.
lm_hie_shrine_text: A hilltop shrine reached through a tunnel of red torii gates. Its guardian monkeys watch over the government district below.
lm_kachidoki_bridge_text: A steel bascule bridge from 1940 whose middle once opened for ships. It has stayed shut since 1970 and now only lifts in old photos.
lm_ameyoko_text: A loud market under the railway tracks in Ueno, born from postwar black-market sweets. Today it sells fish, spices, sneakers and snacks.
lm_national_diet_text: The granite home of Japan's parliament, finished in 1936 after seventeen years of work. Its central tower ends in a stepped pyramid.
piskvorkyRules1: Tap a square, tap it again to place your mark.
piskvorkyRules2: Five or more in a row in any direction wins.
piskvorkyRules3: A quick win earns three stars.
ctyriRules1: Tap a column to drop a disc.
ctyriRules2: Four in a row – across, down or diagonal – wins.
ctyriRules3: A full board is a draw.
mlynRules1: Place your nine stones, then move them along the lines.
mlynRules2: Three in a line is a mill: take one of the rival's stones.
mlynRules3: Down to two stones or no move loses. With three you may jump.
reversiRules1: Place a disc so it traps the rival's discs in a line.
reversiRules2: Trapped discs flip to your colour.
reversiRules3: When nobody can move, more discs wins.
lodeRules1: Tap the rival's grid to fire.
lodeRules2: A hit lets you fire again; sink the whole fleet to win.
lodeRules3: Before your first shot you may re-deal your ships.
posuvneRules1: Tap a tile next to the gap to slide it.
posuvneRules2: Put the numbers in order 1 to 15.
posuvneRules3: Match the par for three stars.
kvizRules1: Ten questions about the city, four answers each.
kvizRules3: Nine right answers earn three stars.
prsiRules1: Match the top card by suit or value; tap a card to play it.
prsiRules2: A seven makes the next player draw two, an ace makes them skip, a queen changes the suit.
prsiRules3: Empty your hand first. Three rounds win the game.
srdceRules1: Follow suit if you can; the highest card of the led suit takes the trick.
srdceRules2: Every heart costs a point, the queen of spades thirteen.
srdceRules3: Lowest score wins. Take every point and the others get 26.
kostkyRules1: Roll five dice up to three times; tap dice to keep them.
kostkyRules2: Then write the roll into one free box of your table.
kostkyRules3: After thirteen rounds the higher total wins.
praseRules1: Roll as long as you dare; every roll adds to your turn.
praseRules2: Roll a one and the whole turn is lost. Bank to keep the points.
kulecnikRules1: Drag from the white ball the way you want to shoot: the direction aims, the length sets the power.
kulecnikRules2: Pot your group, solids or stripes, then the black eight.
kulecnikRules3: Pot the eight too early, or with a foul, and you lose.
bowlingRules1: Slide the ball along the line, then flick it towards the pins.
bowlingRules2: Ten frames of two balls; a strike or a spare earns bonus pins.
bowlingRules3: A spare or strike in the tenth frame gives a third ball.
minigolfRules1: Drag from the ball the way you want to putt; longer means harder.
minigolfRules2: Sand slows the ball, water costs a stroke.
minigolfRules3: Six holes. Finish close to par for stars.
hadRules2: Eat to grow. Every few bites it gets faster.
hadRules3: Don't hit the walls or yourself.
cihlyRules1: Slide your finger to move the paddle.
cihlyRules2: Bounce the ball into the bricks; the edge of the paddle sends it sideways.
cihlyRules3: Three lives. Clear the wall for a bonus.
krtekRules1: Tap the moles as they pop up.
krtekRules2: Golden moles score triple. Leave the bombs alone.
hokejRules1: Move your mallet with your finger and strike the puck.
hokejRules2: Score in the slot at the top; guard the one at the bottom.
driftRules1: Drift inside the ring: handbrake into a slide and hold the angle.
driftRules2: Bigger angle and more speed score more; a long drift raises the multiplier.
driftRules3: Any crash loses the combo you are holding.
driftGallery: Drift zone is played in the city: 90 seconds in a ring on an empty lot.
sprintRules1: Race to the destination; drive through every gate in order.
sprintRules2: Between gates any shortcut is fine.
sprintRules3: Beat the par time for three stars; crashes add seconds.
sprintGallery: Sprint is played in the city: from the start line to a real destination.
stickballRules1: Tap the band where the ball comes in, right as it arrives.
stickballRules2: Perfect timing hits it over the street; late or early is a foul or a miss.
stickballRules3: Leave balls outside the zone alone. Six outs end the game.
doubledutchRules1: Tap on the beat to jump the two ropes.
doubledutchRules2: On a trick beat swipe up instead.
doubledutchRules3: Three trips and you are out; the ropes keep getting faster.
testDriveOver: Test drive over, back in your own car
testDriveNoTaxi: No taxi shift during a test drive
introLine1: Drag your thumb left and right to steer.
introLine2: Drag down to brake, up to boost. A second finger is the handbrake.
introLine3: The phone at the top right: a feed of minigames, the map and trips to other cities.
introCity: Where do you want to drive?
ogTitle: Metropole (GTT) – free driving through real cities
ogDescription: New York, Prague and Tokyo in your browser. Minigames from a feed, no violence.
